walkthrough:
Set The Scene In The Mitochondrion**
Oxidative phosphorylation happens on the inner mitochondrial membrane, folded into cristae to give a huge surface area for carriers and ATP synthase. The starting fuel is reduced NAD and reduced FAD made earlier in glycolysis, the link reaction and the Krebs cycle. They carry hydrogen to be oxidised here, so oxidation means losing hydrogen / electrons.

Split Hydrogen And Move Electrons**
When reduced NAD / FAD are oxidised, hydrogen is released and splits into protons ($H^+$) and electrons ($e^-$). The electrons are passed from one ETC carrier to the next, such as cytochromes, falling to lower energy levels. That is the oxidative part - electrons lose energy step by step.

Build A Proton Gradient**
The energy released by the electrons is used to actively pump protons from the matrix into the intermembrane space. Because the inner membrane is impermeable to protons, they cannot leak back freely. This builds a high concentration of protons in the intermembrane space, so an electrochemical proton gradient is set up across the membrane.

Make ATP By Chemiosmosis**
Protons then diffuse back down their gradient through ATP synthase, the stalked particle protein channels. The flow of protons releases energy which ATP synthase uses to phosphorylate ADP, joining ADP + inorganic phosphate ($Pi$) to form ATP. This coupling of electron flow to ATP formation is phosphorylation.

Keep The Flow Going With Oxygen**
At the end of the chain electrons would pile up and stop the whole process, so oxygen acts as the final electron acceptor. It takes the electrons plus protons from the matrix and is reduced to form water ($1/2 O_2 + 2H^+ + 2e^- -> H_2O$). That is why oxygen is needed for aerobic respiration to continue making large amounts of ATP.

Final answer: Reduced NAD / FAD pass hydrogens to the electron transport chain on the inner mitochondrial membrane / cristae. Hydrogen splits into electrons and protons. Electrons pass along ETC carriers / cytochromes, releasing energy used to pump protons into the intermembrane space, setting up a proton gradient. Protons diffuse back down the gradient through ATP synthase, providing energy to synthesise ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate. Oxygen is the final electron acceptor, combining with electrons and protons to form water.

walkthrough:
Understand What The Respirometer Measures**
Living larvae take up oxygen for respiration and release carbon dioxide. If both gases changed, pressure would hardly change. KOH or soda lime absorbs all the $CO_2$, so any fall in gas volume pulls the coloured liquid drop along the capillary. Distance moved in a given time therefore reflects volume of oxygen taken up.

Set Up Fairly And Safely**
Place a known mass / number of insect larvae in the tube on gauze or mesh above the KOH, so they are not in direct contact with the alkali which is corrosive. Seal the apparatus. Place the whole respirometer in a water bath to maintain a constant chosen temperature and leave a few minutes to equilibrate so expansion or contraction from warming does not move the drop.

Take A Standard Reading**
Use the tap to open the apparatus briefly, then mark the initial position of the liquid drop. Close the tap, start a stopwatch and leave for a set time, for example 5 minutes. Measure the distance moved by the drop in mm with a ruler. Open the tap to reset the drop back to the start before the next reading.

Vary Temperature And Replicate**
Repeat the measurement at at least four different temperatures, for example 10, 20, 30 and 40 degrees C, keeping all else the same such as mass of larvae, time, volume of KOH. At each temperature carry out at least three replicates and calculate a mean to improve reliability and allow anomalous results to be seen.

Calculate Rate And Display Trend**
Calculate respiration rate as distance moved divided by time, e.g. $rate = distance / time$ in $mm$ $min^{-1}$. Plot a graph of mean rate against temperature to show the effect. You would expect rate to rise with temperature as enzymes and kinetic energy increase, then fall if high temperature denatures respiratory enzymes.

Final answer: Place larvae on gauze above KOH in respirometer tube, KOH absorbs CO2 so drop movement shows O2 uptake. Place in water bath at set temperature and equilibrate. Mark initial position of coloured liquid drop, leave for set time, measure distance moved. Reset with tap. Repeat at 4 different temperatures with at least 3 replicates, calculate mean distance / time as rate and plot rate against temperature.
